statements.markdown: the strongest published protocol in each
statements.note: At $k=1$ and sufficiently large $N$, exactly one of Zalka’s $m$ blocks contains a target. It has marked fraction $m/N$, which fixes the weak-check schedule even though the block is unknown. The same schedule can run in every block, and empty blocks never click. Figure S7 reports the combined ZK+WG baseline.

statements.note: In Figure S7, Shirobokov et al. compare the prior protocols in the same asymptotic, zero-error metric and choose the lowest baseline coefficient at each setting. They divide it by the solution’s upper coefficient to report the speedup.

statements.section: Boundary regime (m = 1 or k = 1; BBHT, ZK, WG).
statements.markdown: which avoids discarding the amplified state when a check misses
statements.note: Fang and Heunen’s calibrated weak check retains an amplified state after a miss. Amplifying to a smaller angle costs fewer setup rounds but makes each click less likely. In the small-target-fraction limit, the minimum leading expected cost occurs when the amplification angle is $\pi/4$.

statements.markdown: running all $m$ registers independently over the full domain
statements.note: Each of the $m$ registers searches the full domain and returns a candidate at the same stopping angle. One parallel membership round can check all the candidates. Restarting when all fail adds only a bounded expected number of checking rounds at fixed $m$, so those checks do not change the leading $\sqrt N$ coefficient.

statements.markdown: we evaluate a concrete two-pass schedule
statements.note: After the first pass, the total remainder $R_1$ bounds the remaining count in every block. At a stage set to $s$, any block with exactly $s$ targets yields one with certainty. Every block then has at most $s-1$ targets. Induction down from $R_1$ shows that the second pass clears them all.

statements.section: E.3 Algorithmic mechanisms in verified circuits
statements.note: The Find-Any circuit combines joint amplification of the odd-parity component with a weak check that continues from a miss. The reported gain compares the resulting algorithm with the published baseline. The paper reports a joint ratio for these changes.
